posts.author: daveycadaver
posts.body:
I've spent hundreds. I wanted to spend millions.
In an ideal world, a great game pays for itself through word of mouth. Unfortunately it seems that we live in an era of gatekeepers that won't even mention something cool or indie until it becomes popular through other means and THEN they'll say, "oh... yeah... I played that way back when...".
Honestly... it feels like pulling teeth to even get a review (even a negative one) on Steam... despite thousands of people actively buying your game.
I don't know much but I'm following this thread in the hopes that I'll learn something.

posts.author: Zia_
posts.body:
daveycadaver said:
In an ideal world, a great game pays for itself through word of mouth. Unfortunately it seems that we live in an era of gatekeepers that won't even mention something cool or indie until it becomes popular through other means and THEN they'll say, "oh... yeah... I played that way back when...".
Click to expand...
I don't think, that's how things go. Most people are just too lazy to write reviews or even click some stars, but that has always been the case.
The indie bubble (doesn't matter if games or music or whatever) is always connected to a lot of luck. "In an ideal world", as you phrase it, so with a perfect quality game that is worth playing, everyone should be out there having a wide audience. But most will never get the traction necessary to even get the chance of being seen.
In a realistic world, 9 out of 10 games lack quality unfortunately. And many people aren't willing to dig through it, to find the one exception. If it happens, algorithms (e.g. from Steam) will notice, and snowball it to greater success, because the game will be more visible, will be recommended more ... That's the luck part. But it's not like people out there play the game secretly and plot an agenda to not tell anybody.
About the Marketing - the question in
how
to spend it might be even more important than
how much
. How do you promote an RPG Maker game? In general you can blow out $10.000 or $1 million budget in bad marketing without any effect. But you can push a product even with $1.000 by a lot with good marketing.
For my game I'd look for ways to make it as visible as possible. Spread it as wide as possible. Hand out free keys to streamers to play it for free and raffle some keys for their communties. Be realistic, go to smaller streamers, as the million-follower-ones aren't in the need of indie game support. But smaller Streamers might be grateful. Offer them to be around when they play. Whatever might be appealing. And if it has an effect on popularity, it can be stepped up anytime.
And for those who are thinking about a Kickstarter campaign, should at least consider if they should spend their Marketing budget on promoting the Kickstarter project rather than the actual game. A successful Kickstarter campaign is worth quite a lot, as you have a playerbase from day 1, that will push you into all Newcomer algorithms.

This is a side note to help you. In the early days of Guild Wars 2, we didn't get as quickly reviews as we wanted, so we made this little event review function in the top right corner. Players could say if they liked the quest or not. This is a picture of the beta. In the final version, I think we added the theme skin to it, but it has been a while.
You could make your own with something using
GameAnalytics
. You can use JS and connect it to an eventlistener. Aggregate your feedback and maybe give the player a small incentive for feedback. If they aren't saying anything to you, they might consider the game ok. If there was something bad, they would probably give a bad review and if it was really good they would give that. RPG Maker isn't covered as one of the default engines on GameAnalytics, so when I get to that section then I'll consider making a public plugin for it because it can help a lot of developers. It is probably pretty easy to setup.
Getting back with marketing, I had looked up on Streamer analytics on how much they are paid, and many streamers around 100k subscribers were doing sponsorships for around $200-$300, but it still depends who is the streamer.
Google Trends
or
VidIQ
seems good for knowing general analytics. According to
SocialBlade
, around 100k views is $50 on YouTube. Using Google Ads can be more effective in some cases since you get targeted demographic analytics and avoid dedicating funds to a particular video.
MrBeast
and
Viva La Dirt
do great sponsorship, but I am unable to get any closing numbers on their sales conversions. MrBeast is something like $10k to $1m for mention a game depending on the channel and details. Someone online said TikTok ads are cheaper than Google, but I heard the app might be banned soon and I'm often risk avoidant. Something about sending data to China. Anyways, without knowing sales analytics, no platform seems any better than the other. That smells like trouble to me. Just guessing, but if an Instagram model could get 250k with 0.01% conversion (25 sales) for $200 vs YouTube game streamer getting 100k views with a 1% conversion (1000 sales) for $50, it would make YouTube significantly better.
Upinfluence
can help remove some hassle for return on investment (ROI), but I have yet to try it. Still, some people still swear by word-of-mouth sales, but I can't attach any analytics to it.
I'm vaguely interested in an affiliate marketing program, but also quite skeptical. Usually, they get wide reach to audiences, but rarely close. Throw in like $10k and get $1k back, but that fails to reflect all affiliate marketers. Somewhere out there, there is probably a kindhearted hard seller.

posts.author: Roocifer
posts.body:
Age old saying, it takes money to make money.
When I worked in corporate related jobs and needed to do sales (hated it), I learned from my supervisors and clients what worked and what didn't when it came to selling and how. But for an indie game? I found some gems from fliers handed out at conventions to full on playable demo's at said cons.
Anime Expo for example, had the new Final Fantasy online game package for people to "try" (but it was just signing up and watching a video vs actual playing). They did it as a stamp rally because those are big things at cons right now! Mini scavenger hunt. Basically, you took a picture of their set up and posted it to social media, stamp. Go sign up and watch the video, 2 stamps, with the 3 stamps you got to redeem a goodie bag.
Artists do it where they do themed merch and people find them, buy something, and get a reward at the end. It's how artists market themselves by leeching onto other users social numbers (I say that in the most friendly way possible lol).
If irl events aren't your thing, you can reach out to the Lets Play community on youtube and offer the game for free in return of a video shout out or see about sponsoring a video where you get x amount of time of them talking about your game (usually includes a discount code for the followers). I got some neat codes that way but I have no idea what they charge, it's not very openly discussed.
At the end of it all, word of mouth. If you got a solid game, people will talk about it and come. That's how stardew landed on my radar, my friend told me about it and man that was a fantastic game.
Marketing is a BEAST but if you have to shovel money into it to sell, either the marketing is hitting the wrong demographic or, unfortunately, it's not something for a wider audience and stick to niche markets.
When in doubt, facebook and IG ads.
Edit for budget price: $1000 starting, demo wise. Do pre-launch events. $100 a week after for basic ads and once you start getting traction, either hike yourself up to reach farther or go less, and gather data on if those who play are bringing in their own numbers (word of mouth). You have to play with the waters first before you can solidify on a monthly budget. And if your profits are good, use some of that to funnel into marketing, so the game pays for itself basically.

posts.author: chris-cote
posts.body:
Marketing budget only makes sense if you have something. Don't think of it as an "if I spend X, I'll get Y results) thing. If your game has no legs on it's own, then spending money on marketing will have awful returns. If the game has clear potential (ie. posting about it leads to interest, and the people who do play it enjoy it), then spending can be a multiplier for that traction.
If your concept is good, key art is good, you have some good trailers posted, the Steam page looks nice, and the game is in a genre that people actually want to play, then there will always be some amount of word of mouth interest, and making social media posts of your own will get you some kind of traction.
If your efforts are leading to some amount of interest, then scaling up to do some paid marketing could do something for you, though I would wait until close to launch to do anything paid, and only after the game is on track to be successful. That said, things like facebook ads etc. are not that great. You need organic marketing (running social pages, posting frequently, working with content creators, paid promo, etc.). Your best bet if you have an actual budget is to hire a marketing firm that specializes in this sort of thing to produce content and run your accounts.
If your game has promise and is doing things on its own, I would say the best spending option at that point is paying content creators to play the game. This can have a great return if the game is a good fit with their audience.
All that is to say, if you post your game on social media, and you have a demo up online and nothing is happening, your problem is not marketing in the budget sense. You either need to improve something about the game, or you need to work on the quality of your key art, trailers, game description, etc. Those elements are the initial "gatekeeper" which will cause people to bounce right off your game.
Also, if you don't have a Steam page and a playable demo, do that before you bother with any marketing. You are throwing time and money away until those are done.

There will be marketing managed by my publisher when the game is closer to release, but that hasn't happened yet. All of the marketing so far has just been me.
So far, my game's marketing has been a few trailers and devlog videos on YouTube and the Steam page itself. That was just to get it out there, and the wishlists etc. have come from word of mouth. Some fairly large content creators have played the demo, and this has lead to others finding it, and so-on. As far as marketing goes, I would say that I could have done a lot more than I have. Finding a publisher has allowed me to shift focus away from marketing while I finish the game, knowing that more will come later, but for anyone not working with a publisher, organic posting will be the make-or-break factor on top of making a great game that presents well and has a good demo.
Personally, I would not bother with boosted posts. Organic posting will always outperform this, and even if you get more attention via boosting, it is not going to be valuable engagement. If a post is good and finds its audience, the algorithm will boost it. If a post can only be seen by paying, then it's probably not worth boosting. I don't think social ads will tell you if there is interest in your niche. The communities that surround that niche will tell you, if you go to them. If you're going to pay for anything, I'd suggest you pay for content creators to play the game, and then see what they and their communities think of it. That will tell you far more than a boosted ad. That said, just cold emailing a lot of content creators can be just as effective as paying. If they like it, they'll play it, and if they don't, that tells you something.
If your game is niche, you'll need to go to that niche. Post in their communities, use relevant tags, follow devs who have found success and copy what they are doing and where they are posting, and find ways to stand out amongst your peers. Email content creators in your niche.
